node.label: Lisa McGirr
node.date_label: Suburban Warriors (2001) · “The Passion of Sacco and Vanzetti:A Global History” (2007) · The War on Alcohol (2015)
node.description: A historian of American politics and collective action whose work joins grassroots conservatism, Prohibition and transnational protest. Her Prohibition interview explains selective enforcement and federal coercive expansion while refusing to make the1920s a sufficient cause of today’s prison system.

incident_edges.relationship: Reinterprets Prohibition as consequential state-building and political realignment.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Own interview describes expanded enforcement while expressly denying it alone caused the later carceral state.

incident_edges.relationship: Shows Prohibition enforcement becoming an instrument of white Protestant supremacy and unequal coercion.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Own Herrin answer identifies Klan recruitment and selective action against ethnic/religious targets; one locality is not presented as every locality.

incident_edges.relationship: McGirr explicitly credits Cohen’s Chicago research while placing greater weight on Prohibition and the election of 1928 in the formation of cross-ethnic political loyalties (2016).
incident_edges.evidence_note: McGirr’s own answer to the Making a New Deal question. She calls the emphases distinct but not incompatible; this is an acknowledged debt and extension, not a claim that she repudiates Cohen or derives all her work from her.

incident_edges.relationship: McGirr explicitly agrees with Gerstle’s account of the American state as unevenly powerful, connecting public/private authority and federal tensions to Prohibition (2016).
incident_edges.evidence_note: Own answer on the weak-state myth names both Gerstle and Novak. This link records her specific agreement with Gerstle’s formulation; Novak is not merged into him. Agreement alone does not prove transmission, so the link stays undirected.
